Raids on the House of Cricket Players 
*221. SHRIMATI SAROJ DUBEY: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the house of some cricket players as well as other concerned 
prominent persons were raided for possessing property disproportionate to 
their income; 
(b) if so, the names of the such persons; 
(c) the details of the items recovered from the houses of such persons; and 
(d) the details of the action Government are going to take against them? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI V. 
DHANANJAY KUMAR): (a) Searches have been conducted u/s 132 of LT. 
Act on the houses of some cricket players as well as other connected persons. 
(b) A list of such persons in annexed in the statement (see below). 
(c) Assets of value totalling about Rs. Four crore have been seized. Papers 
and documents have also been seized. 
(d) Necessary action in accordance with the provisions of law has been 
initiated.

training programme for the in-service personnel-1998; 
Environmental Monitoring of Water Resources Projects-1998; and 
Various aspects relating to Dam Safety. 
The third meeting of National Water Resources Council held on 6th February 1996 
considered a number of policy documents prepared by the National Water Board. 
The fourth meeting of the National Water Resources Council was held on 7.7.2000 
to consider the updated draft National Water Policy (1998) and the National Policy 
Guidelines for Water Allocation Amongst States.

consensus among the States on most of the i ssues contained in the proposed policy. 
However, in order to achieve greater convergence and agreement on some contentious 
issues, the Council decided to constitute a Working group including Minister of all the 
States/UTs under the .chairmanship of H on'ble Minister of Water Resources. The 
Council also decided that the draft Nationa l Policy Guidelines for Water Allocation 
amongst States be first considered by the Working Group to arrive at a consensus.

BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): 
(a) to (c) The All India Regional Rura l bank Employees' Association has been 
submitting various Memoranda making se veral demands. A Memorandum dated 
15.02.2000 was received making the following demands:

Circulation of Fake Currency Notes 
†l763. SHRIMATI SAROJ DUBEY: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the fact that people are facing difficulties 
due to the problem of circulation of fake currency notes on a large scale in the country; 
(b) if so, the steps taken by the Government to check the same; and 
(c) whether Government are going to change the design and colour of notes? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) to (c) There are complaints about circulation of fake 
currency notes in the country. However, the total quantity of fake notes recovered/seized 
is only a miniscule proportion of the total not es in circulation. But the Government is 
serious in the matter and has taken the following steps in this regard:—  
(1) A High Level Committee has been constituted to go into the entire gamut of 
issues pertaining to the security dimension of Indian currency. 
(2) A six-member Fact Finding Committee under the convenorship of a Deputy 
General Manager, Reserve Bank of India, comprising of experts on note-
printing/currency paper, etc., has been set up for examining the seized fake 
notes to enable the Government to take remedial action vis-a-vis printing and 
security features. 
(3) The Reserve Bank of India has undertaken a publicity campaign about security 
features incorporated in the genuine notes. 
(4) The security features of Rs. 500 denomination notes have been widely 
published in the print and electronic media to help the people to detect fake 
notes. 
†Original notice of question was received in Hindi.  
91 

RAJYA SABHA [8th August, 2000] 
(5) A film on security features of Rs . 500 denomination notes produced in 
English, Hindi and other regional languages is being repeatedly telecast on 
Doordarshan. 
(6) For the benefit of public a booklet has been brought out which, inter-alia, 
describes the features of genuine notes. This booklet has been placed on 
RBI's website, www.rbi.org.in, besides being available to the public ai RBI's 
Issue Offices. 
(7) The Central Bureau of Investigation has created a special unit for exclusive 
investigation of counterfeit currency note cases. 
(8) The Border Security Force has alerted its troops to be more vigilant in 
checking the smuggling of notes across th e border. Instructions have also 
been issued to all State Governments particularly, border States, to be more 
vigilant. 
(9) A third series of Rs. 500 rupee note in the new. colour .scheme with 
additional security features is in the final stage of approval and these would be 
issued shortly. Initially, these notes are proposed to be issued to the public in 
exchange for the 500 rupee notes issued  in 1987, i.e., those with Ashoka 
Pillar watermark in which forgeries have been detected.

1777. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the Minister of FINANCE be

KUMAR): (a) and (b) Following are the important recommendations made by NIPF in its 
report on 'Reform of Inter-State Sales Taxation in India': 
(i) The maximum rate of CST may be reduced to 3% w.e.f. April, 2001 to 1% from the

102 

[8th August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(ii) Amendment of the CST Act to provide for taxing of declared goods at more than one

(iv) Amendment of the CST Act to delete items falling under Additional excise duty in lieu 
of sales tax (AEDILST) from the list of declared goods; 
(v) Discontinuance of the rental arrangement between the Central and the State 
Governments in respect of AEDILST. 
(vi) Delegation of the power to collect the tax on a number of localized services to the State 
Govts, that would retain the proceeds; and

such time the representation of persons  belonging to the reserved categories 
reached the prescribed percentage of reservation; and 
(b) if so, the services under the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company 
Affairs and all other Orga nizations under its control where the representation

Sabharwal's case (AIR 1995 SC 1371 at page 1375), has held that the operation of the

Comprehensive plan for judicial reforms 
1812. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of LAW, JUSTICE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have chalke d out any comprehensive plan for 
judicial system reforms during the current year and the Ninth Plan period; 
(b) if so, the details of major policy decision taken recently in this direction; and 
(c) what has been the response of State Governments to the reform proposals 
including financial autonomy to judiciary? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF INFORMATION AND 
BROADCASTING AND MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF LAW, 
JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI AR UN JAITLEY): (a) to (c) Judicial 
reforms are a continuous process. Various st eps have been taken by the Government 
for the speedy disposal of both civil and criminal cases. These include amendment of 
the Civil Procedure Code and the Code of Criminal Procedure, increase in the number of 
posts of Judges/Judicial Officers, establishment of Special Courts/tribunals, 
appointment of Special Judici al/ Metropolitan Magi strates and adoption of alternative 
modes of dispute resolution, such as, arb itration and conciliation. Lok Adalats have 
been given a statutory base as supplementary forum for resolution of disputes. There is 
increased use of Information Technology in courts in the country. 
The Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 1999 after obtaining the assent of 
the President is awaiting notification. The Criminal Procedure Code (Amendment) 
Bill, 1994 is under consideration of Parlia ment. The Law Commission in its 154th 
report has recommended a number of measures  for the speedy disposal of criminal 
cases. Such of recommendations which do not require any amendment of law or statute 
have been forwarded to the State Governments/UT Administrations for necessary action 
at their end. The State Governments/UT Administrations are also periodically 
requested to take necessary action to e xpedite speedy disposal  of cases involving 
under-trial prisoners on the basis of Supreme Court's directions in this regard. 
During the current year an amount of Rs. 74.95 crore has been allocated under the 
Centrally Sponsored Scheme for the devel opment of infrastructural facilities for the 
Judiciary for the construction of court buildings and residential accommodation for 
judges and judical officers. This is higher than the allocation 
130 

[8th August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
under the Scheme during previous years.  The XI Finance Commission has also 
recommended an allocation of Rs. 502.90 cr ore for setting up of 1,734 additional 
courts which are expected to clear about 2 million criminal cases during 2001-2005. 
Periodically matter is taken up with th e State Governments regarding judicial 
reforms concerning them and the grant of more financial powers to the respective 
High Courts. Most of the State Governments have taken steps for judicial reforms. 
Some of the State Governments like Karnataka, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, 
Sikkim, etc. have delegated more financial powers to their respective High Courts.

131 

RAJYA SABHA [8th August, 2000] 
and repeated General Electi ons, no important and concrete action has been possible 
after the last batch of electoral reforms in 1996 [The Representation of the People 
(Amendment) Act, 1996] except for some piecemeal measures, like expanding the 
category of employees to be enrolled for election duties [The Representation of the 
People (Amendment) Act, 1998] and making provisions for postal ballot facility for 
migrant voters [The Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 1999]. The 
Government is working out modalities for enacting a fresh batch of electoral reforms. It 
intends to bring very soon a Bill seeking to  extend the current constitutional embargo 
on undertaking fresh delimitation of electoral constituencies upto the year 2026 AD, a 
consensus in respect of which was arrived at in the meeting of political parties held on 
13.5.2000. Further, with a view to enable the members of the armed forces to exercise 
their right of franchise effectively at elections as the present option available to them 
to vote in person or through the system of postal ballot has not proved effective due to 
their posting in distant and remote places and other various reasons, the Government 
has decided to provide an additional option to them to vote through the system of proxy 
at elections. A Bill, namely the Election Laws (Amendment) Bill, 1999, was 
accordingly introduced in the Lok Sabha on 9.12.99 which stands referred to the 
Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs for examination 
and report. The other proposals on electoral reforms are, however, still in the process of 
taking concrete shape. Electoral reforms are an ongoing process and can be carried out 
only after evolving political consensus. The Government intends to continue interaction 
with political parties on various proposals to carry forward the process of electoral 
reforms.

them 119 PAFs are likely to resettle in Gujarat. Thus a total of 3155 PAFs from Madhya 
Pradesh and Maharashtra are likely to be resettled in Gujarat at EL 110.0m, for whom 
the agricultural land requirement for resettlement is 6310ha. against which Gujarat has

Consensus on National Water Policy 
1860. SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that National Wa ter Resources Council (NWRC) could not 
adopt the new National Water Policy because of lack of consensus among the States; 
and 
(b) if so, what are the salient features of the new revised National Water Policy 
and what are those issues on which there were disagreement among the States? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES 
(SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Draft Revised National Water Policy, among others, provides for:— 
(1) Laying greater emphasis on the improvement of the performance of the existing 
water resources facilities. 
(2) Formulation of guidelines for water allocation amongst the basin States keeping 
in view the national perspective on the water resources availability. 
(3) Review and amendment of the Inter-S tate Water Disputes Act of 1956 for 
timely adjudication for Water Dispute referred to the Tribunal. 
175 

RAJYA SABHA [8th August, 2000] 
(4) Establishment of appropriate rive r Basin Organisations with statutory 
powers for the planning, development a nd management for a river basin as a 
whole or sub-basins, where necessary. 
(5) Development of a standardized  national information system for 
promoting free exchange of data among the various agencies through a suitable 
legislation. 
(6) Formulation of a national policy on resettl ement and rehabilitation so that the 
proiect-affected persons share the benefits through proper rehabilitation. 
(7) Enactment of a dam safety legislation to ensure proper inspection maintenance 
and surveillance of existing dams. 
(8) Ensuring institutional arrangements fo r maintenance of water resources 
schemes and involving Water Users Associations in the operation, maintenance and the 
management of water infrastructures. 
(9) Fixing of Water charges for various uses in such a way that they cover at least the 
operation and maintenance costs with well targeted subsidy. 
 
(10) Maintaining minimum flows in the perennial strems and treatment of effluents 
to acceptable levels and standards before discharging into rivers for maintaining 
ecology. 
(11) Encouraging Non-conventional methods for utilisation of water such as 
through inter-basin transfers, artificial recharge of ground water, desalination of brackish 
or seawater, rain water harvesting and watershed management. 
The 4th meeting of the National Water Re sources Council under the Chairmanship 
of Hon'ble Prime Minister was held on 7th July, 2000 for the adoption of revised 
National Water Policy. During the meeting, the deliberations established a broad 
consensus among the states on most of the issues contained in the proposed policy. 
However, some of the areas of differences were as under:—  
(1) Formulation of guidelines for water allocation amongst States. 
(2) Amendment of Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956. 
(3) Establishing appropriate river Basin Organisation with statutory powers. 
(4) Legislation for developing standa rdized national information system. 
In order to achieve greater convergence and agreement on these issues, the Council 
decided for the constitution of Working group including Ministers of all the 
States/UTs chaired by Hon'ble Minister of Water Resources.

Having spent nearly 49 years in the field of law, I may say, Mr. 
Chairman, that a judicial inquiry is not a panacea and it is not the ultimate in 
finding the truth. Mr. Chairman, when our Supreme Court was inaugurated, the 
then Chief Justice spoke and then the doyen of the Bar, Mr. Setelvad, spoke. He 
said, "We shall earn reverence for this institution through truth." We want to 
find, the Government is determined to fi nd, the truth. After the Prime Minister 
spoke, as he spoke, we should not have .the slightest doubt about the 
determination of the Government to find the truth and to resolve and rectify the 
problems. But we must have patience.  Without patience, democracies can 
never function. Democracies do not function and cannot function by being 
impulsive. It would be impulsive at this stage for any one to suggest that we 
must immediately jump into the arena of a judicial inquiry. Surely, there may 
be a good case for a judicial inquiry or there may not be a good case for a 
judicial inquiry.   But this is not the time.

firing and other things, even judges may not be available in the country 
because our country is like a sub-continent. 
DR. L. M. SINGHVI: Sir, I have found that judicial inquiries are a way 
of avoiding a decision. Dr. Johnson used to say, "You appoint a committee in 
order not to take a decision." You appoint a judicial inquiry to arrive at the truth 
swiftly and efficatiously. We may have a judicial inquiry for certain kind of 
issues. It all depends on the type of issues that have arisen. Here, the issue is 
primarily concerned with public order. T hat puts it squarely, constitutionally-
speaking, in the domain of the Go vernment of Jammu and Kashmir. 
Supposing, after ascertainment of the fa cts, they come to the conclusion that 
there are other issues of national secu rity' -- no one can deny that there are 
issues of national security — supposing, they come to the conclusion 
afterwards that it would be better to have a judicial inquiry or any such kind of 
inquiry, there would certainly be a time for it. What has happened is ghastly, 
what has happened is tragic, what has happened is on account of a concerted 
plan of an enemical nature by people who are hostile to us, by people who 
want to destroy amity and  harmony. My distinguished friend, Dr. Karan Singh, 
has rightly said that the Amarnath Yatra was a pilgrimage. I think, a 
psychological moment was seized by our enemies to attack that Yatra and to 
take a heavy toll of life. Only a few days earlier, Mr. Pranab Mukherjee and 
myself happened to be together in Srinagar.       We did have a feeling that this 
was one possibility
